Q: How can I connect to AWS IoT Core MQTT over WebSocket from browser A:

Browsers cannot use X.509 certificates, so to connect to AWS IoT Core MQTT from a browser you must use MQTT over WebSockets (WSS) with SigV4 authentication.

Steps:

  1. Create an AWS IoT Thing and attach a policy allowing iot:Connect, Publish, Subscribe, and Receive.

  2. Use Cognito Identity Pool to obtain temporary AWS credentials.

  3. Connect to your IoT endpoint (*-ats.iot.<region>.amazonaws.com) using MQTT over WebSockets.

  4. Use AWS IoT Device SDK for JavaScript (v2) in the browser.

Why WebSockets?
WebSockets support SigV4 auth, which is required for browser-based connections.

This is the recommended approach by AWS for browser clients.

Q: encryption and decryption algorithm in Rails A:

Starting from Rails 7, encryption of db columns is supported out of the box.
See https://guides.rubyonrails.org/v7.0/active_record_encryption.html.

It boils down to:

creating keys:

bin/rails db:encryption.init

Put the generated keys in your credentials or environment.

Declare attributes as encrypted:

class Article < ApplicationRecord
  encrypts :title
end

Q: Which is the best data type for createdDate and modifiedDate for mongo collection to store dates in database of spring boot application with java 17 A:

Use Instant or ZonedDateTime. Definitely do not use LocalDateTime.

ZonedDateTime adds additional abilities about conversion between geographical zones. Therefore ZonedDateTime is a better choice only if you have to handle zone conversions within your backend. If not then Instant is my default choice as it is the simplest one. Instant handles the reading of the dates with times from your mongodb and to expose them with the standard ISO 8601 format in the endpoint without any additional effort .

Q: Why does assigning `box.content = box` result in `box.content.content` also existing? A:

I think it'd be more natural if the second expression evaluated to false, pointing to the empty chineseBox object defined earlier.

It's not empty anymore. As of chineseBox.content = chineseBox, it now has a property.

When you assign object references to things (variables, properties, etc.), the value stored is a reference to the object, not a copy of it. So both chineseBox (the variable) and chineseBox.content (the property) point to the same object, which has a property called content.

Let's throw some ASCII art at this:

var chineseBox = {};

That gives us:

┌───────────────────────┐
│ chineseBox (variable) │
├───────────────────────┤          ┌───────────────┐
│ value                 ├─────────▶│    (object)   │
└───────────────────────┘          ├───────────────┤
                                   │               │
                                   └───────────────┘

Now we do

chineseBox.content = chineseBox;

...and we have:

                                            ┌───────────┐
┌───────────────────────┐                   │           │
│ chineseBox (variable) │                   ▼           │
├───────────────────────┤          ┌───────────────┐    │
│ value                 ├─────────▶│    (object)   │    │
└───────────────────────┘          ├───────────────┤    │
                                   │  content      ├────┘
                                   └───────────────┘

There's just one object. There are two references pointing to it.
